moment: app knowledge in, alert fires out — the five `*.define` commands and the stream they make possible
source: JOS-482 (cutover ledger item 2 + the fires stream; boundary verdict 3 and owner ruling 22)
note: WHAT THE APP SAYS THE MOMENT IT CONNECTS, in the order it says it, and what comes back when a rule matches. The five commands are the whole of boundary verdict 3: the settings store stays persistence truth app-side and the engine never reads a settings file, so every preference the fold used to read out of it is PUSHED. Each is an idempotent FULL-SET REPLACE — the payload is the whole of what that family knows, so pushing twice is pushing once, a crash-respawn is a replay of the latest push, and the input stays hash-friendly for ruling 18's eventual cache key. THEY GO BEFORE THE ATTACH, which is the shape a real launch has and the only timing that keeps a fold reproducible: all five change what a fold PRODUCES, so a world that took them after the historical scan would have folded the log under one set of rules and served it under another. The ack is the same `DefineAck` for all five; `count` is the entries taken for a LIST payload and absent for the two families that push one object, which is why `buffTrust.define` and `respawn.define` answer without it. NOTE THE ALERT DEFINITION'S EXTRA FIELDS — `volume` and `speech` here — and that the protocol says nothing about them: the field set is the STORE's contract, and a definition round-trips through the fold as the alerts module's published `defs`, so a typed wire shape that dropped an unlisted field would rewrite the user's alerts in transit. THE FIRE AT THE END is what ruling 22 buys: the engine evaluated the pushed rule against a LIVE event and says so. It carries NO `id`, because a fire belongs to the world rather than to any subscription (the epoch-message precedent), and NO `epoch` either — every other stream frame describes window state a client has to reconcile across a generation, while a fire is a thing that happened once, with nothing to drop and nothing to re-request. It is FULLY RESOLVED server-side (the conCard principle): `sound` is `<packId>/<soundId>`, the key the renderer's sound cache is already keyed by, so the app needs no copy of the rule set to make the noise.
